summary.text: 弟 commonly means “younger brother” or “junior.” Early forms are interpreted as a binding around an implement. One proposal is that the graph was reused for the sibling word because the implement’s name sounded similar, but neither the name nor the sound match is established.

formation.text: Pictographic: early forms are interpreted as a binding around an implement, variously identified as a weapon shaft or a peg. The proposal that orderly binding suggested sequence and then sibling rank is an interpretation; no earlier sequence sense is securely dated here. A separate possible account is phonetic borrowing: the graph may have been reused for “younger brother” if the implement’s name sounded like the sibling word, but that sound match is unverified.

components.text: 弟 is treated here as one proposed picture of a binding around an implement, not as a proven combination of modern components. The object is interpreted variously as a shaft or peg. Early forms are described with an element identified as 必/柲, while some bronze forms are described with 弋; no sequence among these shapes is established.

history.text: Oracle-bone, bronze, and Chu manuscript forms are reported, but a continuous graphic sequence to the modern form is not established. The Shuowen account describes successive leather bindings and says the graph follows an ancient form; this is a historical explanation, not a verified reading of the earliest picture.
In 第, 弟 serves as a phonetic component. This sound role belongs to 弟 within 第; it does not make 弟 itself a phonosemantic compound.

Japanese word history distinguishes native oto/otōto from the Chinese-derived reading てい. A cited use from 712 applies oto to a younger person of either sex; the narrowing of おとうと to a younger male sibling is described as an Edo-period development. This is Japanese word history, not a meaning development of the Chinese character.

uncertainties.text: The proposed implement’s spoken name is not established. Reuse of its graph for “younger brother” because the words sounded alike is therefore a possible borrowing mechanism, not a demonstrated sound match.

The early forms do not establish an early “younger brother” meaning. A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟, though its exact date is unresolved; an earlier sequence or rank use is not established.

senses.period: Western Zhou bronze inscription evidence; exact date unresolved
senses.text: A cited Western Zhou bronze inscription uses 弟 in 兄弟. This is the earliest securely sourced sibling use here, but it does not show that the earliest oracle-bone forms already had this meaning.

senses.gloss: junior; younger person or lower in rank
senses.text: 弟 is used for a younger person or one junior in status. When this use began, and whether it developed from the sibling sense, is unresolved.

senses.period: Attestations cited from a Tang poem and later literature; witness dates not checked
senses.text: In literary contexts, 弟 can serve as humble self-reference among peers. Its earliest use and path from a junior designation are unresolved; this sense does not show that the character originally meant “I.”
Classical citations are reported for female younger-sibling or junior uses. Their dates and relationship to the broader junior sense are unresolved.

developments.text: Humble self-reference may be pragmatically related to a junior or younger-peer designation, but the pathway and earliest use are unresolved.

limitations.text: The binding-to-sequence account is an interpretation, and no independently dated sequence or rank use earlier than the sibling sense is established. A semantic chain between these senses cannot be specified.
The evidence gives separate readings and senses, including an ethical 悌-related use, but does not establish a unified development connecting them to the common sibling meaning.

One proposed explanation is that the graph was reused to write “younger brother” because the word for the depicted implement sounded like the sibling term. This is graph borrowing for a different word, not a demonstrated semantic development from “implement” to “younger brother”; the implement’s name and the sound match are not established by the evidence inspected.

evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese University of Hong Kong)
evidence.field: 形義通解；字形序列；《說文》；《廣韻》
evidence.text: The database records two oracle-bone forms, nine bronze examples among eighteen catalogued, and twelve Chu bamboo-and-silk examples. Its scholarly account reads early forms as a rope wound around 柲, a weapon shaft, or in some bronzes around 弋, described there as a peg. Following Xu Hao, it proposes that orderly wrapping suggested 次弟 (sequence), then extended to sibling terminology. It also cites the Western Zhou bronze inscription on the 殳季良父壺, with 弟 in 兄弟. These are the database’s interpretations and cited evidence, not a visually verified reading of the glyphs in this research.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 弟

evidence.source: 臺灣教育部《異體字字典》
evidence.text: The dictionary gives the Shuowen account: 弟 means the successive order of leather bindings and follows an ancient form; its cited old-text variant is analyzed there as abbreviated ancient 韋 plus 丿 as phonetic. Its entry quotes classical sources separately by sense: sequence/rank is cited from 呂氏春秋 and 漢書; younger brother from 爾雅, 左傳, and 史記; younger sister/female junior use from 孟子 and 史記; and humble self-reference to a peer from a poem attributed to Tang poet 王季友 and 紅樓夢. These references establish transmitted textual attestations, not the date of surviving manuscripts. The entry presents the 悌-related ethical reading under a separate pronunciation and gives 論語 and 禮記 examples.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》— 弟

evidence.source: 《說文解字》, electronic transcription at Wikisource
evidence.text: Xu Shen’s account, preserved in this transcription, explains 弟 as the successive order of leather bindings and says it follows the appearance of an ancient graph. This is a historical lexicographic assertion, not independent confirmation of the depicted object or semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 說文解字/05

evidence.field: Chinese: glyph origin; pronunciation; historical phonology
evidence.text: The page labels 弟 a pictogram of a spear handle wrapped in a leather strap and claims the wrapping suggested sequence, extended to younger brother. The same page reports modern Standard Mandarin dì (Pinyin), Middle Chinese dejX in Baxter notation, and Old Chinese *lˤəjʔ in Baxter–Sagart 2014; it reports Zhengzhang 2003 Old Chinese *diːlʔ and *diːls for two readings in the 脂 rime group. These are reconstructions for 弟, not for the pictured implement or its name. Its gloss list includes junior and a literary humble “I/me” between male friends; those senses require separate semantic histories.
evidence.title: 弟 — Wiktionary

evidence.field: Chinese: 弋 glyph origin and pronunciation
evidence.text: The 弋 entry describes the character’s pictographic referent as a sharp peg and gives Zhengzhang 2003 Old Chinese *lɯɡ; its Mandarin reading is yì. This is not the name of a weapon shaft and does not demonstrate a sound match with 弟. The evidence inspected therefore does not independently establish the spoken name or pronunciation of the object depicted in the proposed 弟 analysis.
evidence.title: 弋 — Wiktionary

evidence.field: Chinese: 第 glyph origin and historical phonology
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 第 as a phono-semantic compound: 竹 ‘bamboo’ as semantic element and 弟 as phonetic element; it also notes that sequence may alternatively have been written 弟. It lists Standard Mandarin dì, Middle Chinese dejH, Baxter–Sagart 2014 *[l]ˤəjʔ-s, and Zhengzhang 2003 *diːls for 第. This supports a phonetic role for 弟 within the later graph 第; it does not make 弟 itself a phonetic compound.
evidence.title: 第 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Kotobank, entries from 日本国語大辞典 and 字通

This Japanese semantic history should not be treated as evidence for the character’s Chinese graphic origin.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: The claimed depicted object varies across accounts: weapon shaft, peg, or an element identified as the early form of 柲. No inspected primary image was visually checked, and the object interpretation remains attributed to the specialist database and other secondary accounts.

The independent pronunciation/name of the supposed weapon or tool is not established. Reconstructions for 弟 do not establish the name of a depicted object, so the whole-graph phonetic-loan explanation for ‘younger brother’ is not demonstrated by the sound evidence inspected.

The graphic account that a wrapped shaft/peg represents ordered binding, followed by an extension to sibling rank, is a scholarly interpretation. The inspected sources do not establish a dated independent “order/sequence” lexical use earlier than the sibling use; do not infer that chronology from Shuowen’s gloss or a modern dictionary ordering.

The oracle-bone record shows early forms but no independently checked contextual oracle-bone token meaning ‘younger brother.’ The earliest securely sourced brother use in this research is the Western Zhou bronze example cited for 殳季良父壺, though an exact inscription date was not established.

The distinction between early component readings 必/柲 and some bronze forms written with 弋 has not been resolved as a single ancestor sequence. No source inspected warrants assigning a chronological origin_form relation among these component shapes.

No graphic corruption or palaeographic sequence from the oracle-bone/bronze forms through seal, clerical, and regular forms was independently demonstrated from visually inspected glyph images. Xu Shen’s ancient-form analysis is recorded as a historical account, not automatic confirmation.

The peer self-reference meaning ‘I/me’ is a pragmatic extension from a junior or younger-peer designation; its mechanism and earliest dated use are not established by the checked sources. It is not evidence that 弟 originally meant a first-person pronoun.

The local dossier’s gloss ‘I, me’ needs sense separation: the source checked restricts this to humble literary self-reference among peers, while younger sibling, junior, student/disciple, female younger sibling, sequence/rank, and 悌-related ethical use have separate contexts or readings.
The Ministry source supplies citations to classical works, not manuscript witness dates; dates of surviving witnesses for these cited uses were not independently checked.

The database’s character-form images and the Chinese Academy bronze archive’s object-level page were not directly inspected visually; the archive page timed out. No claims in this result rely on having seen those images.
This invocation did not identify and inspect an individual Xiaoxuetang glyph image record, so no Xiaoxuetang image is proposed despite verifying its CC0 query-interface rights notice.

The Commons 弟-bronze.svg file page was inaccessible in the web tool. Its mirror description indicates a reusable modern vector redraw, but direct provenance and rights were not verified on the primary file page; no image is selected.

The inspected sources report early oracle-bone and bronze forms but do not establish a visually verified continuous graphic sequence or settle whether the early depicted element is a weapon shaft, peg, or binding arrangement.

No independent evidence in this invocation establishes the spoken name or ancient pronunciation of any proposed depicted implement. Reconstructions for 弟 cannot by themselves demonstrate a whole-graph sound loan.

No new dated contextual token for the sequence or sibling sense was established here. Repository dossier evidence reports a Western Zhou inscriptional 兄弟 example, while exact dating and the earliest order-sense attestation remain open.

The exact Commons source pages and imageinfo records for 弟-seal.svg and Shuowen Seal Radical 202.svg could not be opened. Their identity details, provenance, script-period attribution, and license have not been verified from primary file records; neither is selected as a glyph.

The 弋-seal.svg file is a modern vector labeled Shuowen seal style and has explicit public-domain terms, but the image itself was not pixel-inspected and it does not illuminate the early graphic formation of 弟, so it is not selected for the character entry.
The linked ancient-character images on the CUHK database page were not visually inspected. The claims about rope, shaft, and peg remain attributed interpretations, not direct visual findings.

The proposed implement’s spoken name and ancient pronunciation remain independently unestablished. The local rows show 弋 yì (Baxter–Sagart *lək) and 弟 dì (Baxter–Sagart *lˤəjʔ), while the cited entry treats early depicted elements as 必/柲 and sometimes 弋. A reconstruction for 弟 cannot establish a name for the pictured object; no whole-graph borrowing by sound is demonstrated.

The individual official Unicode Unihan records for 弋 (U+5F13), 弟 (U+5F1F), and 第 (U+7B2C) could not be opened. The supplied local kMandarin rows are recorded above as local dataset evidence; Unicode’s official general database overview was inspected but is not a per-character citation.

The seal-vector provenance for 弋 is explicit on its Commons page, but the selected candidate image was not pixel-inspected because retrieving the original SVG returned a cache-miss error. No visual shape description is asserted.

The bronze sibling-use citation is available in the CUHK database, but an exact inscription date and an independently sourced earlier sequence-use attestation were not established in this invocation. Dictionary ordering is not treated as chronology.

Neither exact Commons file page nor the requested imageinfo response was accessible, so no direct image URL, file-specific reuse rights, author, or provenance was verified. No Commons glyph is selected.

The CUHK specialist record provides actual linked historical form candidates, but the web interface did not expose their pixels in this inspection. The account of a rope around a shaft remains attributed to that database; the competing peg interpretation in bronze forms remains unresolved.
The implement’s ancient spoken name and pronunciation are not independently established. Reconstructions for 弟 cannot by themselves substantiate a whole-graph sound loan for the sibling word.
The sources report graph examples from oracle-bone, bronze, seal, and Chu manuscript traditions but do not establish a visually verified continuous sequence to the modern graph.

The historical sources report early oracle-bone and bronze forms, yet their competing readings of the depicted element—as a shaft or peg bound by a cord—remain interpretations rather than a visually verified account of those forms.
